peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewer Comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript by Meader et al. entitled “Bnip3lb-driven mitophagy maintains fate of the
embryonic hematopoietic stem cell pool,” the authors describe how ROS-mediated mitophagy
can increase HSPCs numbers in the CHT expansion niche in zebrafish. In particular, they
identified a role for receptor-mediated mitophagy via Bnip3lb rather than pink/parkin stress-
induced mitophagy in the process. While the data provided mostly support the author's
conclusions, some facets require further substantiation.
Author response: Thank you for taking the time to review our manuscript. We appreciate the
thoughtful critiques and recommendations, and hope that you find the changes adequate.
Major points:
1) The authors present data in Figures 2 and 3 to build an argument that mitophagy is a
programmed component of HSPC during the transition from the specification to expansion niche.
Some of the data are difficult to interpret. For example, in figure 2G and H, they claim to have
found a strong bias toward increased expression of mitophagy-associated TF and effectors in the
HSPC fraction. The strong bias is not very apparent from the data presented. Can statistics be
applied? Violin plots with accompanying adj. p-values showing the difference in expression
between the HE and HSPC clusters could better illustrate the point.
Author response: We have significantly expanded and adapted our analysis to provide a more
robust, statistically grounded demonstration of mitophagy-related transcriptional upregulation in
embryonic HSPCs. Our original submission presented findings from a 36hpf scRNAseq dataset,
during the peak of HSPC specification in the aorta. We have now expanded this analysis in the
revised submission, by adding another dataset from a later time point, 48hpf, to further underscore
the developmentally-timed metabolic switch and its functional consequences as HSPCs bud from
the ventral dorsal aorta (VDA) and seed the caudal hematopoietic tissue (CHT). We have also
significantly updated our analysis of each dataset: both the 36hpf and 48hpf scRNAseq datasets
were reprocessed using a standard and fully documented Seurat workflow, including log-
normalization, selection of variable features, scaling, Principal Component Analysis, construction
of a shared nearest-neighbor graph, clustering, and UMAP embedding (Figure 2a-b). Clusters
were recoded into biologically interpretable labels (EC, HEC, HSPC, Ery, Mac, MSC, Neut, NP)
based on differentially expressed genes (Supp. Figure 2a-b), and validated with canonical
HSPC, myeloid, erythroid and endothelial lineage markers, including: cxcr4b, gata2b, itga2b,
runx1, spi1b, lyz, mpx, gata1a, hbbe3, klf1, cdh5, kdrl, and tie1 (Supp. Figure 2e-f). To quantify
lineage-related transcriptional programs, we computed module scores (Figure 2c-d) for curated
endothelial (cdh5, kdrl, tie1), HSPC (cxcr4b, gata2b, itga2b, meis1b, mpl, myb, notch1b, runx1,
spi1b), and myeloid (lyz, mpx, spi1b) gene sets using Seurat’s AddModuleScore. (Supp. Figure
2c-d). We performed differential expression analyses using FindMarkers in Seurat (default
Wilcoxon test) comparing HSPC clusters against HECs or ECs. GSEA was performed using
clusterProfiler’s gseGO with the zebrafish Gene Ontology annotation (org.Dr.eg.db). Expression
of mitophagy- and hypoxia-related genes (e.g., bnip3, bnip3la, bnip3lb, fundc1, pink1, park2,
hif1aa, hif1ab) was directly examined within the HSPC cluster at each timepoint (Figure 2e-
f). To harmonize raw UMI counts between datasets, we downsampled RNA counts from selected HSPC
clusters using DropletUtils downsampleMatrix to a target of ~4,600 UMIs per cell.
At 36hpf, in addition to downregulation of genes associated with endothelial identity/function when
HSPCs are compared to HECs or ECs by GSEA pathway enrichment, we see a significant
enrichment in metabolic signatures and ROS/redox related pathways (Figure 2c). By 48hpf, we
no longer detect a distinct HEC fraction, matching the kinetics of hematopoietic development
where endothelial identity is further downregulated as HSPCs bud from the aorta and transit to
seed the secondary “expansion” niche in the CHT.1 Interestingly, while the enrichment in
metabolic/mitochondrial pathways (Figure 2d) is retained, we no longer see a strong signature
for ROS/redox response, suggesting that as HSPCs mature, they may be inducing pathways to
control environmental “stressors” like ROS. Due to the pronounced increase in metabolic state
and mitochondria-related pathways, we profiled mitophagy-related genes within the HSPC cluster
to determine if the machinery was present and therefore potentially able to contribute to the
regulation of ROS/stress response within the HSPC pool. Specifically, we looked at the
expression of pink1, parkin, fundc1, bnip3, bnip3la, and bnip3lb within our datasets (Figure 2e-
f), as well as related transcriptional regulators hif1aa and hif1ab. While expression of several
mitophagy related genes increased between 36 and 48hpf, we found that bnip3lb was the highest
expressed within the HSPC fraction. To validate these observations, we performed qPCR analysis
for each gene in sorted populations from Tg(cmyb:EGFP;kdrl:Has.HRAS-mCherry) transgenic
reporter embryos, inclusive of Endothelial (Kdrl+/Myb-), Myeloid (Kdrl-/Myb+) and HSPC
(Kdrl+/Myb+) fractions, finding the strongest enrichment for bnip3lb and pink1a in HSPCs (Figure
3f, Supp. Figure 3f-k). Through modulation of Hif1α activity and ROS levels (Figure 3k-m, Supp.
Figure 3m), we identified Bnip3lb as the more physiologically relevant regulator of mitophagy
during developmental hematopoiesis, and confirmed a distinct regulatory role for bnip3lb (vs
pink1) through MO knockdown studies for impact on CD41lo HSPC formation (Figure 4h-j, Supp.
Figure 4d). We believe that the combination of our expanded bioinformatics analysis and
validation studies now more definitively supports the spatio-temporal induction of mitophagy
during HSC formation.
Additionally, in figure 3, it is extremely difficult to see what cells were analyzed in the mitoQC
reporter assays, as the reporter is expressed everywhere. It is unclear how they ensured the
signal quantified was only in kdrl+ cells? Flow cytometry might be more sensitive to detect the
mcherry-to-gfp ratio in the kdrl:BFP+ cells to ensure the signal quantified is in the right cells. The
quantification using the cd41:mitoQC partially alleviates these concerns.
Author Response: We concur that using either the MitoKeima and MitoGR reporter lines, “red-
only” expression indicative of mitophagy is present in other cells within the VDA region
(representative sample for: MitoKeima - Figure 3b; MitoGR - Figure 3c); this includes nearby
floor plate and muscle, as well as red blood cells in circulation within the lumen of the aorta and
vein, which have been previously shown to utilize developmental programmed mitophagy during
their maturation, and serve as a positive control for the tool at this timepoint.2 To that end, we
utilized an established Tg(kdrl:TagBFP) pan-endothelial cell reporter3 to aid identification of
endothelial cell (EC) fractions within the VDA region, inclusive of hemogenic endothelium (HEC)
and newly specified HSPCs; we have now included a detailed description in the methods for the
“masking” performed in Imaris using the BFP+ marker in the confocal images to localize
evaluation of mitophagy to the EC/HEC/HSPC fraction (see page 17). Interestingly, in regard to
the ECs lining the dorsal aorta and posterior cardinal vein, we only observed the presence of
mitophagy puncta in rounded or “budding” cells along the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta across
multiple independent biological samples using two distinct reporter lines (5 replicates for
MitoKeima (Figure 3b); 4 replicates for MitoGR (Figure 3c)), which are presumptive HEC/HSPCs
based on their location and morphology.1 While these images were only intended to illustrate
localization of mitophagy positive cells within the hemogenic niche, in the prior submission and
revised figure (Figure 3d), we did employ confocal-based analysis for mitophagy activation using
the MitoGR tool in the Kdrl:BFP+ population to distinguish the proportion of mitophagy positive
cells in the VDA versus CHT, showing a statistically significant increase in the latter. The
“mitophagy index” shown on y-axis of that graph was calculated using the same mathematical
method as that published previously by our collaborators4; for clarity, we now directly indicate it is
an assessment of the red/green ratio within the BFP+ fraction to help define the methodology in
the figure, legend and text. Please note, to enhance consistency with the prior publication and
construct design, we adjusted the MitoQC label to MitoGR throughout.
As the previously established in vivo mitophagy reporter systems utilize both GFP and mCherry
fluorescent channels, we were unfortunately unable to specifically co-localize the presence of
active mitophagy with well-characterized HSPC reporter lines, such as the Runx1+23 transgenic
reporter5 - a highly conserved marker for newly specified HSCs in the dorsal aorta niche at this
stage of development - for which we have only red and green tools available. Given that caveat,
and our reliance on Kdrl:BFP-labeling, it was challenging to definitively quantify differences in
ECs/HECs versus budding HSPCs in the VDA at 36hpf by confocal using the mitophagy index
methodology, as described in Wrighton et al.4, which is essentially a ratio of puncta volume/
tissue volume. Following presentation of refined localization of mitophagy gene expression to the
HSPCs versus ECs by qPCR in subsequent figure panels (Figure 3f, Supp. Figure 3f-k), we
provide quantification of changes in MitoGR reporter activity within presumptive HSPCs after
genetic or compound-mediated perturbation compared to matched controls using the mitophagy
index score (Figure 6a-b) or manual counts of mitophagy positive puncta (Figure 4b-c).
As suggested in the review, we did attempt to perform FACS analysis using the CD41-driven
MitoGR line that we developed to further assess numbers of HSPCs undergoing mitophagy at
48hpf. However, the low number of total CD41 positive cells in the whole embryo (using 10 pooled
embryos per sample) prohibited clear visualization of individual gated red and/or green
populations at sufficient signal strength over background to calculate a statistically meaningful
mitophagy ratio. Therefore, we believe our quantitative analysis of the confocal imaging is the
best way to illustrate changes in HSPC-related mitophagy in vivo between treatment groups.
2) In the human iPSC experiments presented in Figure 7, the authors show less ROS in the cells
treated with NR. This phenotype is the opposite of what is expected from the literature and their
work in zebrafish. Is it possible that altering NAD+ levels is working via a non-ROS and non-
mitophagy means? To link these data to the findings in the rest of the paper, the authors need to
demonstrate whether the NR effect is mitophagy/ROS independent or dependent.
Author Response: Based on prior publications6,7, we expected to see a decrease in ROS after
treatment with the mitophagy-stimulating agent NR. There are a number of ways that NR has
been shown to impact ROS levels, including NAD+ modulation (as indicated) and upregulation of
SIRT1, impacting antioxidant gene expression.8 To help clarify this point for the reader, we have
changed the text on page 12 to say “However, NR was noted to reduce intracellular ROS levels
in all cultured cells as measured by CellROX at this timepoint (Supp. Figure 7c).“
To further address the role of mitophagy in NR-driven impact on ROS-mediated HSC regulation,
we performed an additional set of epistasis experiments in zebrafish embryos. Bafilomycin
treatment can be used to block the lysosomal fusion that is necessary for completion of
mitophagy.9,10 Embryos were treated with NR, Bafilomycin, or a combination of both agents from
48-72hpf; we found that when progression of mitophagy was disrupted by Bafilomycin exposure,
NR stimulation was no longer able to increase HSPC numbers in the CHT (Figure 7a). We
repeated this experiment with an alternative mitophagy-stimulating agent, FCCP, which is thought
to act via a distinct method from that of NR (via alterations in proton gradients11), and found
essentially the same results (Figure 7b). Together, this indicates that ROS-associated impact on
HSC number can be regulated by modulation of mitophagy in general. While we cannot formally
rule out that NR treatment would not also enhance relevant antioxidant gene expression to help
maintain or amplify regulatory impact on ROS, we did find that NR stimulation was unable to
increase HSPCs over wild-type levels in the setting of bnip3lb knockdown in zebrafish, suggestive
of redundant and/or compensatory balance.
To further document that the effect of NR on HSPCs is mediated via mitophagy in the culture dish,
we have now additionally utilized FCCP during in vitro iPSC to HSPC generation. For direct side-
by-side comparison of impact, we utilized both NR and FCCP treatment in replicate studies,
employing a newly published and refined iPSC to HSC differentiation platform (termed the “Loh”
protocol) in which phenotypic HSPCs can be reliably produced over a 10-day protocol. NR and
FCCP were applied in the media when “floating cells” (indicative of EHT) began to appear in the
culture to most closely phenocopy the dosing window in fish (Figure 7h). Once “budding” HSPCs
were generated, they were isolated from the media and utilized in serial CFU assays to assess
their self-renewal and differentiation capacity. We found that NR and FCCP treatment each
enhanced serial CFU production (Figure 7j), in line with our prior observations for NR, with a
significant increase in the multipotent GEMMs noted for both treatments. Consistent with our
zebrafish work, this indicates the effect on HSPC expansion is mediated through mitophagy more
broadly, and not just an effect of NR treatment. Of note, as the “Keller” protocol utilized in the prior
submission is now understood to primarily produce cells with short-term HSPC-like function, that
data has been moved to Supplemental Figure 7.
Additionally, in Figure 7G, the secondary plating effect is quite promising, but it looks mostly like
an expansion of CFU-G not the multipotent GEMMs. These data suggest a role for NR on
differentiation rather than HSPC maintenance/self-renewal. Please clarify.
Author response: Thank you for this important point of clarification. We did not continue to
expose the cells undergoing the serial CFU assay to the mitophagy-stimulating compounds after
the initial dose during differentiation culture. As such, in the secondary replating, we would not
necessarily expect to see either maintenance or further expansion of multipotent GEMMs, which
are presumably being stimulated to differentiate via the cytokines included in the CFU media.
However, if transient NR exposure during hematopoietic specification and EHT successfully
expanded production and/or maintained GEMMs through the first round of plating, those cells
would then be present in sufficient number to functionally read out as increased hematopoietic
colony output in the second round of plating compared to matched control, which is indeed what
we observed (Supp. Figure 7d-e). Importantly, in the revised submission, we observed similar
effects on total colonies and GEMMs for both NR and FCCP treatment when we independently
replicated the serial replating assay using mitophagy-stimulated cells derived from the Loh-
derived protocol (Figure 7j), underscoring the utility of mitophagy in HSPC maintenance.
3) While the use of a grading system to define the amount of ISH signal as a means to quantify
the amount of HSPC or differentiated blood cells within zebrafish embryos/larvae is common
practice, more robust quantification is warranted. To further support their claims, the authors need
to use appropriate statistics such as Chi-squared tests for all graphs denoting phenotypic
distributions.
Author response: We have now performed Chi-square analysis of the phenotypic distributions
for all WISH data presented in this manuscript as suggested. Furthermore, we made sure to
further support conclusions drawn from WISH analysis through use of a corresponding
quantitative method such as flow cytometry or qPCR to increase the robustness of our claims.
4) The majority of the experiments testing bnip3lb in zebrafish are performed using a single
morpholino. It is also important to provide an independent validation of the ROS-mediated effects
by bnip3lb. Performing the NAC epistasis experiment using an independent bnip3lb morpholino
would further support this major conclusion of the manuscript. This is especially important as
elevated apoptosis and diminished proliferation are implicated in the diminished HSPC levels in
bnip3lb morphants. Both of these cellular processes can be mediated by Tp53, a pathway known
to be aberrantly upregulated by some morpholinos.
Author response: To address potential concerns regarding utilization of a single bnip3lb MO,
we have now included analyses for several of the foundational experiments, including effects on
HSPCs at 72hpf and epistasis with NAC, with a second independent bnip3lb MO, as requested
(Figure 4I, Supp. Figure 4c, Supp. Figure 5f). We also generated bnip3lb crispant embryos to
further validate effects on HSCs (Figure 4j, Supp. Figure 4h); we see corresponding decreases
in HSCs whether using the splice or ATG bnip3lb MO, or the crispant embryos, each of which are
now included in the revised manuscript in Figure 4h-j for comparison.
The authors did assess HSPC levels in an established bnip3lb mutant but instead of lower levels
as seen in the morphants, the mutants showed higher levels of HSPC in the CHT. They argue
this is due to genetic compensation, but the data are not so clear. The observed that knockdown
of bnip3la in bnip3lb mutants lowered HSPC levels to near wildtype levels, but it did not result in
diminished HSPC levels similar to what was observed in the morphants.
Author response: Thank you for pointing out this discrepancy between the data shown in the
figure and our claims in the text. A review of the relevant data revealed a transposition error in
the final version of the graph utilized in Supplemental Figure 4 for the bnip3lb mutant. After
reanalysis of the data from this experiment and an additional repetition for appropriate statistical
application of the requested chi-square analysis (Supp. Figure 4e-f), as well as qPCR analysis
for expression of alternative mitophagy mediators (Supp. Figure 4g), we are now able to better
demonstrate the suspected gene compensation, consistent with our prior statement.
Another way to illustrate that morpholino effects that are different from mutants are still from on-
target effects on the gene of interest is to inject the morpholino into mutants. If the morpholino
effect is on-target, then the morpholino phenotype should be suppressed in the mutants.
Author response: As indicated in the response above, we have concerns regarding probable
genetic compensation in the bnip3lb mutant embryos. For that reason, we prioritized the design
and application of a second MO and the production of new crispant embryos, which together
consistently demonstrated the same HSPC phenotype (Figure 4h-j) and further support the
validity and specificity of our findings for Bnip3lb-mediated mitophagy in this process.
Also, there is an incomplete description of the bnip3lb mutant in the manuscript or in the cited
paper from Wrighton et al. Please add more information on the type of mutation in the mutant.
Author response: We apologize for this oversight and are happy to provide additional information
regarding the bnip3lb mutant line, which was initially developed for use in the investigation by
Wrighton et al.4 The method used for the creation and validation of each of the mitophagy mutant
lines was identical to those described in the text for bnip34, based on a previously published high-
efficiency Crispr genome editing protocol.12 While the targeting sequences for bnip3 and bnip3la
were listed in the published supplementary table of the Wrighton paper, the bnip3lb mutants were
not yet established as a stable line and therefore not included in the final publication. The targeting
sequences for creation of the bnip3lb mutant allele are now indicated in the methods and
Methods Key Resources table; successful mutation was validated by Sanger sequencing as
previously described13.
Minor points
1) To help orient the reader, please add experimental schemas and time points to the figures.
This especially important for figures with multiple developmental stages and different treatment
paradigms.
Author response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have now added a more informative
schematic in Figure 1a. This figure now includes colored arrows to indicate the relevant treatment
windows. To help orient the reader throughout the paper, we have now included corresponding
colored text to any figure with precisely timed dosing to better showcase the distinct window(s) of
application. Furthermore, we have explicitly stated dosing windows for each experiment in the
results and figure legends to aid experimental clarity and interpretation.
2) Related to Figure 1B- the main text says 48 hpf but the figure says 72 hpf. Please make sure
they match and list the correct developmental time point when the experiment was performed.
Author response: This was an unintentional formatting hold-over from a prior draft of Figure 1.
We have corrected the main text to indicate “72hpf” to match the labeling and CellROX data
presented in the final version of Figure 1b, as well as ensured that it is indicated correctly in the
corresponding figure legend (page 5, first paragraph).
3) In Figure 1E, please provide example flow cytometry plots to illustrate how low vs high cd41:gfp
was defined.
Author response: We have added representative flow plots for the CD41:GFP analysis (Supp.
Figure 1d), as well as the first use of other flow cytometry analyses employed throughout the
paper [i.e. Rag2:GFP (Supp. Figure 1e) and Mpx:GFP (Supp. Figure 1i)] to Supplemental
Figure 1. The same gating strategies were applied for all zebrafish flow cytometry data presented
in subsequent figures employing each of these same transgenic lines.
4) In Figure 1G, it is hard to see the KM in the images so please provide better images. Also
quantification should be included to support the claim.
Author response: We have replaced these panels with images taken by confocal microscopy to
increase resolution (see updated Figure 1g). Due to its complex positioning at the head/body
junction and lack of a secondary reporter line to clearly delineate the tissue boundaries (vs cells
nearby in circulation), we did not take direct measurements of the fluorescent patterning in the
KM by confocal microscopy. Rather, we performed further quantification of the HSPC effect via
flow cytometric analysis using Tg(cmyb:eGFP) embryos, which are presented as Figure 1h.
5) In Figure S1E, please denote the specific transgenic line used to assess neutrophils.
Author response: We have added the transgenic tool designation for the myeloperoxidase line,
Tg(mpx:gfp), to the text on page 5 in the second paragraph: “Notably, prdx1 morphants showed
minor changes in expression of the neutrophil marker mpx at this timepoint by WISH or via flow
cytometry on Tg(mpx:GFP) embryos”. The appropriate reference is indicated here14 and in the
supplemental methods.
6) In the main text on page 6, the authors state, “GO terms related to biosynthesis, perhaps
reflecting the beginning of their rapid expansion phase.” This statement is quite speculative. It is
also possible that the change reflects the change from stationary to migratory cells ate this
transition. Please soften or remove the statement
Author response: We completely revised the scRNAseq analysis, as indicated in the response
above, and have removed this statement as suggested.
7) In the main text, the authors state “Importantly, by confocal mitophagy of the Tg(ubb:HyPer) in
vivo.” Please correct mitophagy to microscopy.
Author response: Thank you for noting that error. We have corrected this mistake (page 8, first
paragraph), so the sentence now reads “Using an established Tg(ubb:HyPer) ROS reporter line,
ROS levels were unexpectedly found to be significantly decreased by confocal microscopy and
flow cytometry within HSPCs in the CHT, …”.
8) Figure 2F- definition of color scale is missing. Unclear what the comparison is and if the genes
in green are more or less represented in the newly formed HSPC. It is also unclear if the numbers
in the boxes represent fold change or log2 fold change. Please clarify.
Author response: We have eliminated this figure in favor of a more informative analysis and
presentation in the current version of the manuscript.
9) Critical statistics are missing in several locations. For example, Figure 3G- stats should be
included for NAC bnip3lb qPCR; Figure 4A- stats are missing in the comparison of the mitophagy
reporter signal in bnip3lb knockdown compared to controls. Please ensure statistics are included
for all quantitative data.
Author response: We have added the statistical analysis and notation for these figures, which
can now be found in Figure 3j (bnip3lb in con vs NAC), and Figure 4b (mitophagy puncta in
control vs bnip3lb MO), respectively.
10) In Supp Figure 4B, it is very difficult to see the o-dianisidine staining in the larvae. Please use
better images.
Author response: We have repeated this experiment and retaken representative photos of the
embryos as requested. The new images are now included in Supp. Figure 4b.
11) In Figure 4G, the cmyb ISH signal in the pink1 MO is out of focus. Please provide a better
image.
Author response: As data was added to illustrate the specificity of impact of loss of bnip3lb
compared to other mitophagy genes on HSPCs, we focused on validating effects through flow
cytometry to better enhance quantitative evaluation and comparison. In doing so, we eliminated
the WISH photos/distribution for pink1a. Flow data for pink1a MO knockdown on CD41lo HSPCs
is shown in Supp. Figure 4D, along with the data for bnipla, bnip3, and fundc1 MOs.
12) In Figure 5H, the number of cells/embryos analyzed should be included on the figure.
Author response: We have removed the pie chart distributions and added scatter plots with error
bars with each point representing the individual samples analyzed for each condition. Please find

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Meader et al. investigate the regulatory mechanisms of embryonic hematopoietic
stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in maintaining multipotency during rapid proliferation. They
demonstrate that in zebrafish embryos, ROS levels drive initial HSPC specification in the dorsal
aorta, but these levels need subsequent control to prevent apoptosis and differentiation. Bnip3lb-
mediated mitophagy emerges as a key mechanism in this process, reducing ROS during HSPCs'
endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT) and in the caudal hematopoietic tissue (CHT).
Knockdown of Bnip3lb in zebrafish impairs mitophagy, leading to increased ROS, apoptosis, and
skewed differentiation toward myeloid lineages, effects reversible by antioxidant treatment.
Further, activation of mitophagy in human iPSC-derived HSPCs increases their long-term
hematopoietic potential, suggesting therapeutic implications for improving stem cell transplant
efficacy. This study underscores the potential significance of developmentally programmed
mitophagy in stem cell maintenance and suggests strategies to boost HSPC production ex vivo
through controlled mitophagy.
Despite these intriguing implications, the study seems significantly underdeveloped. Notable
limitations include: (1) an over-reliance on qualitative data, (2) insufficient controls for morpholino
studies and lack of alternative methods, and (3) limited validation in the human system, despite
the claims made. Overall, it is unclear whether the central tenet of this paper is adequately
supported by the data presented.

address the broader concerns raised above along with the specific comments listed below. To
address potential over-reliance on qualitative data, we have added both statistical analysis and
an additional quantitative method to confirm phenotypes found in each qualitative experiment. To
address concerns regarding insufficient controls for MO studies and lack of alternative methods,
we have now expanded our controls and incorporated alternative tools to validate our claims.
Finally, we have expanded our assessment of relevance in the human system. The specific
changes are reflected in the manuscript and addressed in more detail below.

the green GFP signal is quenched, allowing only the more pH resistant red mCherry signal to
remain detectable in select cells. In the revised version of the schematic, we have now added a
second series of images to highlight the differences between the two tools, including re-coloring
the initial image of MitoGR mitochondria to more clearly indicate the combined fluorescent
labeling at baseline, and the remaining “red” color post lysosome fusion. In our hands, during
timepoints relevant to HSPC development, the MitoGR line proved more readily quantifiable by
Imaris when utilized in combination with the Kdrl:BFP EC/HEC/HSPC marker, and as such was
used for the mitophagy index calculations shown.
5) The application of these findings to hiPSCs is potentially impactful, but needs to be solidified.

a. Given the broad and potentially varied effects of NR, the authors should confirm that NR
treatment increases mitophagy in hiPSCs.
Author response: We appreciate this concern as NR is known to impact Sirtuin activity16, which
in addition to influencing initiation of mitophagy, can lead to regulation of antioxidant gene
expression8, providing an additional route to control ROS levels. To address this important point,
we set out to create a stable iPSC line expressing a previously described mitophagy reporter;
unfortunately, despite several attempts at introducing the construct, we were unable to establish
a line that consistently documented mitophagy activation in response to biochemical stimulation.
As an alternative approach to validate the beneficial impact of mitophagy on newly specified HSCs
in culture more generally, we exposed cells to FCCP, which stimulates mitophagy through
depolarization of the mitochondria membrane. Importantly, we found a similar enhancement in
HSPC production for exposure to either NR or FCCP in iPSCs (Figure 7j) as well as in zebrafish
embryos (Figure 7b). Furthermore, in the zebrafish model, we confirmed that both NR and FCCP
are mediating their effect (at least in large part) through mitophagy via chemical epistasis
experiments with Bafilomycin, which inhibits lysosomal fusion. When progression of mitophagy is
blocked via Bafilomycin treatment, neither NR nor FCCP stimulation can enhance CD41lo HSPCs
number (Figure 7a-b). A primary role for NR-driven mitophagy was further confirmed in zebrafish
through epistatic investigations with the bnip3lb MO, where NR stimulation was unable to increase
HSPC numbers in the setting of loss of receptor-mediated mitophagy (Figure 7c). Together, our
data indicates that NR is most likely eliciting its primary effect on HSPCs through activation of
mitophagy and subsequent control of ROS levels.
b. Moreover, the beneficial effects of NR in Fig 7 should be BNIP3 dependent to support this
model.
Author response: We would politely disagree with this point. While our zebrafish data indicates
that the primary regulatory program activated in the developmental setting is Bnip3lb-related (with
some modest compensation and/or redundancy from other receptor subunits), we find also that
any exogenous compound-mediated activation of mitophagy, provided that the machinery
necessary to initiate the mitophagic program is present (all components are expressed in iPSC
cells according to https://anglohlabs.shinyapps.io/blood_devcell_shiny), should exhibit a
beneficial impact on ROS levels and maintenance of HSC numbers. To support this conjecture,
we now provide data for both NR and FCCP stimulation and see a similar impact in vitro (Figure
7j). We did also conduct the requested epistasis investigation in zebrafish embryos using the
CD41 HSPC reporter and found that loss of bnip3lb did blunt the ability of NR exposure to
significantly enhance CD41lo HSPC numbers (Figure 7c).
c. Does a general decrease in ROS (e.g. NAC treatment) similarly improve the secondary CFUs
of hematopoetic progenitors, or is there something special about mitophagy’s role?
Author response: We thank the reviewer for bringing up this important point. ROS levels have
been well documented to tip the scale between cell cycling and quiescence17, as well as lineage
commitment and retention of adult HSC fate.18 NAC can be utilized to regulate cellular ROS levels
more generally, both in vivo and in the culture dish19, however, the precise level of ROS that is
needed to allow for HSC expansion, while maintaining multi-potency is not established. Indeed,
prior reports have indicated that in the cell culture setting, as well as in the clinic following stem
cell transplant, complete ROS inhibition has detrimental effects on HSC function and
hematopoietic homeostasis.20 For that reason, we were intrigued by the potential impact of
mitophagy in maintaining HSC state, as its function can be dependent on perceived local
environmental stimulation (both in regard to gene expression of its components and cellular
activation). Our data indicates that transient activation of mitophagy during iPSC differentiation
appears to be sufficient to decrease ROS to an acceptable level to promote self-renewal.

associated mitophagy is not Bnip3lb dependent, but rather stimulates the Pink/Parkin pathway
via damage/stress response activation.21,22 As now more accurately detailed in our analysis, we
find that developmentally programmed/receptor-mediated mitophagy, such as that mediated via
Bnip3lb, appears to be required during HSC development to allow for HSC expansion while
preserving multipotency. However, as long as the pathway components are expressed in the cell
type of interest, we are in fact able to further stimulate HSC production through activation of any
form of mitophagy via transgene induction or compound exposure both in vivo and in vitro.

migrate?
Author response: This is an interesting question. When evaluating these samples, we always
look at the whole embryo in addition to locally in the hematopoietic niche of interest at the time

generally not recognized to have a specific transcriptional signature.

reanalysis of our single cell data, and with the addition of the new dataset, we have eliminated
this analysis altogether. We now perform GSEA and highlight key Gene Ontology - Biological
Process terms along with direct visualization of known mitophagy genes in the HSPC clusters.

enriched. Please specify the unbiased metric(s) used to support enrichment claims.
Author response: Thank you for this important clarification question. We have now reanalyzed
and restructured the scRNAseq expression profiling study to better support our claims regarding
expression within the various niche fractions, inclusive of the HSPCs; we have also incorporated
new data sets to provide additional insight into changes associated with maturation of EC to HSPC
state in the VDA and CHT niche, including a metabolic switch associated with strong upregulation
of oxidative phosphorylation and ROS production (Figure 2c-d). Our data indicates that
expression of mitophagy components increases during the transition from EHT (36hpf) to HSC
expansion (48hpf) in the CHT (Figure 2e-f), with bnip3lb, fundc1 and pink1 showing both the
highest comparative expression in the HSPC fraction (bnip3la is also upregulated in the CHT).
To further investigate cellular specificity, we profiled expression in Kdrl/cMyb-labeled FACS isolated
cell fractions by qPCR (Figure 3f, Supp. Figure 3f-j) and can now more confidently support the
claim that bnip3lb is uniquely enriched in HSPCs during this window of hematopoietic
development in the developing embryo.
6) Pg 12. “…ATG5-dependent autophagy is essential for EHT, highlighting the importance of
multiple autophagic pathways in embryonic HSC production.” Does this imply that BNIP3lb-
mediated mitophagy and Atg5-mediated autophagy are distinct? If so, what evidence suggests
that BNIP3lb-mediated mitophagy is ATG5-independent?
Author response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. While ATG5 is a core
component of the canonical autophagy machinery, several studies have shown that mitophagy
can occur through ATG5-independent mechanisms, depending on the molecular context and the
receptors involved. For example, certain forms of receptor-mediated mitophagy, including those
involving BNIP3 and NIX (BNIP3L), can proceed even in the absence of ATG5, through alternative
macroautophagy routes utilizing other autophagy-related proteins such as ATG6/Beclin1 and LC3
family members.23,24 In our system, Bnip3lb appears to act as the primary mitophagy receptor
utilized during hematopoietic development, but our data do not exclude potential involvement of
Atg5. Instead, our interpretation is that Bnip3lb-mediated mitophagy could function either through
canonical ATG5-dependent autophagy or via compensatory pathways employing other
autophagy-related proteins (e.g., Atg6/Beclin1, as described in erythroid mitophagy). Thus, the
requirement for ATG5 in developmental mitophagy may vary depending on cellular context and
autophagic flux requirements. Importantly, ATG5-dependent autophagy is not specific to
mitochondria and encompasses multiple degradative processes24, whereas BNIP3lb-mediated
mitophagy represents a more selective, developmentally regulated form of autophagy. Therefore,
our data emphasize that multiple autophagic mechanisms, both general (ATG5-dependent) and
selective (BNIP3lb-mediated), contribute to embryonic HSC emergence, underscoring the novelty
of our findings in revealing their coordinated functional impact during EHT. We have now better
highlighted this interesting point in the discussion as it will be an important area for future
investigation.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript, the authors describe the role of Bnip3lb-regulated mitophagy in maintaining
the embryonic hematopoietic stem cell pool in zebrafish. The authors elaborate on how
spatiotemporal control of ROS is important for generating and regulating the HSPC pool. First,
the authors show the essentiality of ROS for HSPC specification in the ventral-dorsal aorta (VDA)
niche but not for HSPC specification in the caudal hematopoietic tissue (CHT) niche. Next, they
claim that Bnip3lb-driven mitophagy regulates ROS within the CHT. Knocking down Bnip3lb
causes a reduction of embryonic HSPC and increased ROS at CHT, which can be rescued by
treatment with NAC. Finally, they present data on how NR-induced mitophagy can be leveraged
to form hiPSC-derived hematopoietic progenitors. This is a potentially very interesting manuscript,
but the data are unfortunately not of sufficient quality to conclude that Bnip3lb-regulated
mitophagy is responsible for the observed phenotypes.
Author response: Thank you for this comprehensive review of the data provided in our original

Major Points

Nevertheless, the consistent HSPC phenotype observed across the expanded tools, as well as

3. Whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH). Throughout the manuscript, they do WHISH for
runx1/cmyb together. Any reason why it is not done individually? The negative controls (using the
sense probe) are missing, and the WHISH staining varies a lot from image to image (e.g. control

Author response: We apologize for any confusion caused by the presentation of the WISH data
and/or rationale for the methodology employed and evaluation of results. We have opted to utilize
combined application of the runx1/cmyb probe set as it helps to delineate budding HSPCs from
other populations present within the ventral dorsal aorta. Runx1 is expressed at low levels on
primitive erythrocytes in circulation, flattened endothelial cells on the ventral wall of the dorsal
aorta which have initiated hemogenic gene programs (but may or may not complete budding), as
well as newly specified HSPCs. At this stage of development, cMyb is expressed on primitive
myeloid populations, and maturing HSPCs budding from the ventral wall of the aorta. As all of
these populations are adjacent in time and space, we generally combine the probes to better
highlight (amplify signal) the beads-on-a-string pattern of the “budding” runx1/cmyb double
positive fraction representative of HSPCs, and not nearby primitive myeloid or erythroid cells or
endothelial cells that may not complete EHT. Both probes have been widely utilized in the field
since the early 2000s25, such that we and others have published numerous reports with them
individually or together (including sense strand controls) to establish the validity of the expected
expression pattern and relevance to our biological process of interest. We have elected to keep
them combined here to more easily compare newly specified HSPCs between embryos; however,
we have now also provided a representative image of the individual WISH probes in the CHT at
72hpf for comparison (Supp. Figure 1c).
Given that zebrafish are not inbred animals, and their development was not artificially
synchronized from time of aqueous fertilization, a bell-shaped distribution of expression levels is
typically observed in untreated, wild-type embryos, hence the utility of scoring animals into these
three relative expression categories (high/medium/low) across replicate clutches. Stained
embryos were directly compared with stage-matched sibling controls within a single clutch to
judge alterations in WISH patterning and intensity, with the exception of embryos from
homozygous mutant incrosses, which were compared alongside matched wild-type clutches as
indicated. At least 20 embryos from a minimum of two independent clutches were analyzed per
treatment condition and/or genotype, with blinded phenotype scoring independently assessed by
at least two lab members; numbers of individual embryos analyzed per condition are now
indicated to replace the previously reported ranges. Images were selected to represent the
median expression pattern observed for each treatment/condition, using embryos from the same
clutch. We have added this information to the methods to provide further clarification to the reader
(page 16). As WISH distribution is a qualitative assessment of expression levels, in addition to
the chi-square analysis now provided for each data set, we have included an additional
independent quantitative assessment by qPCR, flow cytometry and/or microscopy to verify and
further enumerate the phenotypes observed and support the validity of our claims.
Minor points:

Author response: Thank you for pointing out that error, which was a holdover from an earlier

Author response: We have updated the formatting of the ROS analysis to better capture

Is the strong staining observed in the vertebral column true or autofluorescence?

on Zfin.org, as assessed by global expression analysis in the Thisse lab28 (Thisse et al., 2004 -
Fast Release Clones: A High Throughput Expression Analysis: https://zfin.org/ZDB-FIG-050630-

mediated by Hif1α (Figure 3l). Altogether, the data now presented in Figure 6 implies that as long
as the relevant mitophagy machinery is present in the target cell-type, compound-mediated
exogenous activation of mitophagy via stimulatory route is sufficient to drive HSC production
and/or protection from premature differentiation, as determined by increased CD41lo HSPC
numbers by FACS. While not investigated in depth here, we previously demonstrated that DMOG
treatment can enhance HSPC development in the VDA via activation of Hif1α-associated
transcriptional regulation19, which would presumably include the Bnip family as identified here, as
well as a number of other relevant hematovascular targets.30,31

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is
part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide
appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Response to Reviewer Comments – Second Revision
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have sufficiently addressed concerns from the prior submission.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed my comments and concerns in a satisfactory manner and the
manuscript has been substantially improved.
Author response: Thank you for your assistance in reviewing and improving our manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have made meaningful improvements, including stronger quantitative analyses, the
addition of appropriate morpholino controls (including a second morpholino and crispant
controls), and more substantial validation in human systems.
My only remaining concerns include some generally modest effect sizes across several assays,
as well as the lack of direct evidence that the observed phenotypes in human cells specifically

Author response: We are glad to find that you are satisfied with the majority of updates and
extensions included in the revised submission. Regarding the first point raised, while we

it clearly demonstrates that robust production and maintenance of HSCs both in vivo and in vitro

Concerning the second comment, as indicated in the response to the prior review, we agree that

the observed phenotypes in human cells specifically reflect mitophagy (specialized autophagy).
However, as mentioned in the earlier rebuttal, we were able to show that stimulation with either

while we cannot formally exclude beneficial impact(s) from additional mechanisms of action, we

maintenance of iPSC-derived HSPCs. Additionally, as indicated in the comments, whereas a

HSPC numbers in the zebrafish embryo, further supporting our proposed regulatory mechanism.
We have included statements in the discussion (page 13) to further underscore the potential for

“Of note, while similar results were observed for FCCP treatment, which acts via an
independent mechanism to induce mitophagy, NR regulates cellular redox via multiple
pathways and is not specific to mitophagy alone; additional work will be needed to
distinguish the isolated and combinatorial impact of each potential arm of its regulatory
mechanism on HSC fate.”
Minor point: the title of Supplemental Figure 2 (“Expression of mitophagy related genes in flow
sorted HSPC cells”) appears inaccurate, as the figure now pertains to gene expression used to
define cluster identities rather than mitophagy per se.
Author response: Thank you for pointing out that disconnect between the revised supplementary
figure and title. We have now updated it to read:
“Supplemental Figure 2: Identification of the HSPC population within the scRNAseq
datasets (Related to Figure 2)”
